Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

By [F1] the left side of step 1.1 is the pointwise risk, and by [F2] its first term on the right is the variance. This is the asserted identity.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a Borel statistic on $(\mathbb R^2)^n$ with its
product Borel sigma-algebra: each weight, product, and finite sum is Borel;
the positive-denominator set is Borel, and division is continuous there. In
any statistical experiment on this sample space whose pointwise regression
estimand is $\psi_x(\theta)=m_\theta(x)$, with $m_\theta$ the selected
version from [[def-regression-target-version]], it is an estimator of
$\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is
part of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for
bias or variance results are stated in those results.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

Under the global alternative it is uniformly bounded and tends to zero for each fixed $u$: split the remainder integral at $|u|\le A$, use uniform continuity near $x$ on that fixed set, and bound the remaining part by $C\int_{|u|>A}u^2K(u)\,du\to0$ as $A\to\infty$. derivations.claim: For the general assertion truncate $L$ to $L_A=L\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le A,\ |L(u)|\le A\}}$. The expectation of $(nh)^{-1}\sum_iL_A(U_i)$ is $\int L_A(u)f(x-hu)\,du\to f(x)\int L_A$ by uniform density convergence on its fixed compact support. Its variance is at most $(nh)^{-1}\int L_A(u)^2f(x-hu)\,du=O_A((nh)^{-1})\to0$. The elementary bound $\mathbb P(|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(V)/\epsilon^2$ follows by integrating $\epsilon^2\mathbf1_{\{|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon\}}\le(V-\mathbb EV)^2$. Thus the truncated average converges in probability.

The expectation of the absolute difference between the full and truncated averages is at most $C\int|L-L_A|$, using the global density bound or its bound on the shrinking image of the compact support of $L$. This tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Markov's bound, obtained from $\epsilon\mathbf1_{\{Z>\epsilon\}}\le Z$ for $Z\ge0$, makes this difference uniformly small in probability. Also $\int L_A\to\int L$. First choosing $A$ large and then $n$ large proves the general assertion.

For the rapid-tail case and $L(u)=u^jK(u)$, $j=0,1,2$, restrict first to $|x-X_i|\le\delta$, where the density is bounded. The same truncation proof works there. The expected absolute contribution of the remaining observations is at most $\epsilon_h h^{2-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-3}f(z)\,dz\to0$, where $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. Thus the same scalar limits hold for these three moments without a global density bound.

Apply steps 1.1–3.1 to $L(u)=K(u)u^j$ for $j=0,1,2$, all integrable by the finite second moment. Symmetry gives $\int uK=0$. The entries of $M_n$ therefore have the displayed limits. Its determinant tends in probability to $f(x)^2\mu_2>0$, since it is a polynomial in the entries. A zero determinant lies outside a fixed neighborhood of this positive limit, so its probability tends to zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a Borel statistic on $(\mathbb R^2)^n$ with its
product Borel sigma-algebra: each weight, product, and finite sum is Borel;
the positive-denominator set is Borel, and division is continuous there. In
any statistical experiment on this sample space whose pointwise regression
estimand is $\psi_x(\theta)=m_\theta(x)$, with $m_\theta$ the selected
version from [[def-regression-target-version]], it is an estimator of
$\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is
part of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for
bias or variance results are stated in those results.

Assume AC for the chosen regression version [[def-regression-target-version]].
Let $X$ have Lebesgue density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point
$x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative, symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.
Assume either that $K$ has compact support, or that $f,m$ and their first
two derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$. In these first two alternatives, no continuity
or boundedness of $K$ is required. The global alternative supplies tail
control for noncompact kernels; local smoothness alone does not supply it.
A further localization alternative, including the Gaussian kernel, is that
$\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$, $K$ is bounded, and
$$\lim_{A\to\infty}\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)=0.$$
Under this rapid-tail alternative only the stated local smoothness of
$f,m$ is needed; no global boundedness of $m$ or of its derivatives is assumed.
For sufficiently small $h>0$, the population smoother corresponding to
[[def-nadaraya-watson-estimator]] is well defined by
$$m_h(x)=\frac{\int K(u)m(x-hu)f(x-hu)\,du}{\int K(u)f(x-hu)\,du},$$
and
$$m_h(x)-m(x)=\frac{h^2\mu_2}{2}\left(m''(x)+2m'(x)\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right)+o(h^2).$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

derivations.claim: Write $h=h_n$, $Z_i=K((x-X_i)/h)$, $B_i=Z_i(m(X_i)-m(x))$, $T=n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i$, $Q=n^{-1}\sum_iB_i$, $a=\mathbb EZ_1$, and $b=\mathbb EB_1$. In the compact/global alternatives, $m$ and $\sigma^2$ are bounded on the active kernel region for small $h$; thus $\mathbb E[|Y_i|\mid X_i]\le |m(X_i)|+\sqrt{\sigma^2(X_i)}$ is uniformly bounded there. The weighted response average has integrable absolute value, since it is bounded by $\sum_i|Y_i|\mathbf1_{\{Z_i>0\}}$. Conditioning on the predictors gives mean bias $\mathbb E[Q/T;T>0]+(a_0-m(x))\mathbb P(T=0)$. Change of variables gives $a\asymp h$, and [F3] gives $c=b/a=m_h(x)-m(x)=O(h^2)$. Bounded $m$ on the active region yields $|B_i|\le C Z_i$, $\mathbb EZ_i^2=O(h)$ and $\mathbb E(B_i-cZ_i)^2=O(h)$, by $R(K)<\infty$ and the appropriate density bound. Under the rapid-tail alternative, [F6] gives $\int m^2f<\infty$ and $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, so integrability follows from the latter. The bounds $\mathbb EZ_i^2=O(h)$ and $\mathbb E(B_i-cZ_i)^2=O(h)$ still hold: inside a fixed smooth neighborhood $m,f$ are bounded; outside it $K((x-z)/h)^2\le C h^6/|x-z|^6$ and $\int m^2f\le\mathbb E Y^2<\infty$. For $R=Q-cT$, independence gives $\mathbb ER=0$, $\mathbb ER^2=O(h/n)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(T)=O(h/n)$.

Positivity near zero implies there are $A,\kappa>0$ and a Borel set $J\subset[-A,A]$ of positive measure on which $K\ge\kappa$: the positive neighborhood is the countable union of its level sets $\{K\ge1/k\}$. Hence $p_h=\mathbb P((x-X_i)/h\in J)\asymp h$. The count $N$ is binomial. On $G=\{N\ge np_h/2\}$, $T\ge c_1h$. With $\gamma=1-e^{-1}-1/2>0$, Markov's bound applied to $e^{-N}$ gives $\mathbb P(G^c)\le e^{np_h/2}(1-p_h+p_he^{-1})^n\le e^{-\gamma np_h}\le e^{-c_2nh}$. In particular $T=0$ is contained in $G^c$.

On $G$, $R/T=R/a-R(T-a)/(aT)$. Since $\mathbb ER=0$, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $|\mathbb E[R/a;G]|$ by $a^{-1}(\mathbb ER^2)^{1/2}\mathbb P(G^c)^{1/2}$. The second term has absolute expectation at most $C h^{-2}(\mathbb ER^2)^{1/2}\operatorname{Var}(T)^{1/2}=O((nh)^{-1})$. On $G^c\cap\{T>0\}$, $|R/T|\le C$ in the compact/global alternatives. In the rapid-tail alternative [F6] makes $m$ square-integrable, and the squared response-law mean is at most $\sum_i m(X_i)^2+a_0^2$. For each $i$, the event $G^c$ forces the count among the other $n-1$ observations below $np_h/2$; independence and the same binomial bound give $\mathbb E[m(X_i)^2;G^c]\le\mathbb E Y^2 e^{-c_3nh}$. Thus Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its first-moment bad-event contribution by $O(\sqrt n e^{-c_4nh})$. The fallback and the omitted $c\mathbb P(T=0)$ also contribute $O(\mathbb P(G^c))$. Consequently $\mathbb E\widehat m-m(x)=c+O((nh)^{-1})+O((1+\sqrt n+(nh)^{-1/2})e^{-c_5nh})$. Here $(nh)^{-1}=o(h^2)$ by $nh^3\to\infty$, and $nh\ge h^{-2}$ and $nh\ge n^{2/3}$ eventually make the exponential term $o(h^2)$. Substituting [F3] proves the claim.

The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$

product Borel sigma-algebra: each weight, product, and finite sum is Borel;
the positive-denominator set is Borel, and division is continuous there. In
any statistical experiment on this sample space whose pointwise regression

$\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is
part of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic on $(\mathbb R^2)^n$ with its product
Borel sigma-algebra: the matrix entries are Borel, the nonsingular-matrix set
is Borel, matrix inversion is continuous there, and the fixed fallback gives
the other branch. In any statistical experiment on this sample space whose
pointwise regression estimand is $\psi_x(\theta)=m_\theta(x)$, with
$m_\theta$ the selected version from [[def-regression-target-version]], it
estimates $\psi_x$ in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case
$p=1$ is the **local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for
a given sample is implicit in this definition.

Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume AC. Let X,Y take values in standard-Borel E,T, and let K be a disintegration kernel giving the conditional law of X given Y. For measurable $f:E\to[0,\infty]$, put $h(y)=\int_E f(x)K(y,dx)$. Then h is measurable and
$$E[f(X)\mid\sigma(Y)]=h(Y)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

For measurable real f with $E|f(X)|<\infty$, define $D=\{y:\int|f(x)|K(y,dx)<\infty\}$ and use the signed integral for h on D, zero off D. Then $P_Y(D)=1$, h is real measurable, and the same identity holds.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $M_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)\to f(x)\operatorname{diag}(1,\mu_2)$ in probability. Put $V_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)$. The scalar generalization proved in [F3] applies also to a continuous multiplier $\sigma^2(x-hu)$: on fixed truncated support this multiplier converges uniformly to $\sigma^2(x)$ and is bounded, and the tail expectation is bounded by $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}|L|$. Thus, for $L=K^2$ the $(0,0)$ entry tends to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. In the rapid-tail alternative, local truncation remains valid. For $j=0,1,2$ the expected absolute far contribution to $V_{n,j}$ is bounded by $C h^{5-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-6}\sigma^2(z)f(z)\,dz=o(1)$, since [F7] gives $\int\sigma^2f\le\mathbb EY^2$. Also $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ follows from boundedness and the rapid tail. For the local-linear conclusion, $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ permits $L=K^2u^j$, $j=0,1,2$, by the same truncation argument. All entries then converge to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)\int K^2u^{j+k}$; symmetry makes the off-diagonal limit zero. Terms with $K(U_i)=0$ are interpreted as zero. Every active response-law variance is finite almost surely; these are variances under the specified conditional response laws, without an assumption of unconditional square integrability.

On the event $\sum_iK(U_i)>0$, [F1], conditional response independence, and [F4] give $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_{1:n})=\dfrac{\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)}{(\sum_iK(U_i))^2}$. Writing $M_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)$ and $V_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)$ makes the scaled variance $V_{n,00}/M_{n,00}^2$, which converges to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)/f(x)^2$. The zero-denominator event has probability tending to zero by [F3]'s $(0,0)$ entry, so the same convergence holds with the fallback.

On a nonsingular local-linear design matrix, weighted least squares gives conditional variance $(nh_n)^{-1}e_0^\mathsf TM_n^{-1}V_nM_n^{-1}e_0$, where $e_0=(1,0)^\mathsf T$. The limit matrix is diagonal with entries $f(x)$ and $f(x)\mu_2$, so its inverse has first diagonal entry $1/f(x)$; the $(0,0)$ limit of $V_n$ is $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. Matrix inversion is continuous at this invertible limit, because its entries are quotients of entries of the adjugate by the nonzero determinant. Thus the scaled conditional variance converges to $R(K)\sigma^2(x)/f(x)$. By [F3] the singular-design event has probability tending to zero, and the fallback does not change convergence in probability.

For the extra Nadaraya–Watson clause, choose $A,\kappa>0$ with $J=\{|u|\le A,K(u)\ge\kappa\}$ of positive measure, possible since $\int K=1$. Its predictor count is binomial with success probability $p_h\asymp h$. On $G_n=\{N\ge np_h/2\}$, $T_n=n^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)\ge c_1h$, whereas Markov's bound applied to $e^{-N}$ gives $\mathbb P(G_n^c)\le\exp(-c_2nh)$. The truncation argument of step 1.1 also proves $V_{n,00}\to f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$ in $L^1$: the bounded truncated average converges in $L^2$, while the expected absolute tail is uniformly small. On $G_n$, $(T_n/h)^{-2}$ is bounded and converges in probability to $f(x)^{-2}$. It follows that the expectation of the scaled conditional variance on $G_n$ has the stated limit: separate $V_{n,00}$ into its constant limit and an $L^1$ error, and use bounded convergence in probability for the reciprocal factor. On $G_n^c$, the conditional variance is at most the active-region bound on $\sigma^2$, since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, or the fallback is deterministic. Hence its scaled expectation is $O(nh e^{-c_2nh})\to0$ in those alternatives. Under rapid tails, the conditional variance is at most $\sum_i\sigma^2(X_i)$; the count among the other $n-1$ observations is independent of $X_i$ and is below $np_h/2$ on $G_n^c$. Its binomial lower-tail bound gives $\mathbb E[\sigma^2(X_i);G_n^c]\le\mathbb EY^2 e^{-c_3nh}$. Thus the contribution to the expected scaled conditional variance is at most $n^2h\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_3nh}$. Under the stated $nh^3\to\infty$ condition, $nh\ge n^{2/3}$ eventually, so this polynomial factor times the exponential tends to zero.

Let $A_n$ be the response-law mean of the Nadaraya–Watson fit, including its fallback, and let $m_h=\int Kmf/\int Kf$. The kernel integrals and localization or global bounds imply $m_h\to m(x)$. Put $Z_i=K(U_i)$ and $R_n=n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i(m(X_i)-m_h)$. Then $\mathbb ER_n=0$ and $\mathbb ER_n^2\le n^{-1}\mathbb E[Z_1^2(m(X_1)-m_h)^2]=o(h/n)$: after change of variables, continuity at $x$ handles a fixed compact $u$-set and the integrable $K^2$ tail is dominated by bounded $f,m$. On $G_n$, $A_n-m_h=R_n/T_n$, so its expected square is $o((nh)^{-1})$. On $G_n^c$, $A_n$ and $m_h$ are bounded in the compact/global alternatives. Under rapid tails, [F7] gives $\int m^2f<\infty$; the far part of the second-moment integral is $O(h^6)\int m^2f=o(h)$, and the leave-one-out binomial argument in step 3.1 gives $\mathbb E[A_n^2;G_n^c]\le n\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_4nh}+a_0^2\mathbb P(G_n^c)$. Its expected squared bad-event contribution is therefore negligible in all stated cases, and $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)\le\mathbb E(A_n-m_h)^2=o((nh)^{-1})$. Bounded active-region means and variances, or the bound $\widehat m^2\le\sum_iY_i^2+a_0^2$ under rapid tails, make the Nadaraya–Watson fit square-integrable. Expanding its centered square and integrating first under the response laws gives total variance equal to the expected conditional variance plus $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)$. Step 3.1 therefore proves the unconditional Nadaraya–Watson expansion.
